column2: A small chip that is combined with others in one package to build a larger processor. Quantum chiplets let big systems be built from smaller, higher-yield pieces.
column3: In classical computing, chiplets are used the same way to build large processors.

column2: IBM's qubit connectivity pattern, a hexagonal lattice with extra qubits on the edges, so each qubit has two or three neighbours. It reduces crosstalk and frequency collisions.
A qubit connectivity pattern based on a square lattice with extra qubits on the edges, lowering each qubit's number of neighbours.
A layout in which qubits sit on a honeycomb or hexagonal grid. It is used by some processors and codes, such as the honeycomb code.
A link that connects qubits on separate chips or modules, so a processor can be built from several smaller modules.
Moving trapped ions between zones of a trap by changing electrode voltages, used to bring ions together for gates in QCCD architectures.
A package holding several quantum chips connected together, so they work as one larger processor.
A link that uses photons in fibre or free space to connect quantum modules, for example ion traps or atom arrays, into a larger system.
Moving quantum information between locations by sending it as photons, instead of physically moving qubits.
A shared element, such as a resonator or a common motional mode, that couples several qubits so they can interact.
A trapped-ion architecture in which ions are moved between dedicated zones on a chip for storage, gates and measurement. Quantinuum's machines use it.
Any link that transfers quantum states or entanglement between separate quantum devices, such as a fibre or microwave link.
A layout in which each qubit connects to four neighbours on a square grid, as needed by the standard surface code.
A crossing point in a trapped-ion chip where ions can be routed between different arms of the trap.
A region of a trapped-ion chip with a specific role, such as storage, gates, loading or measurement.
A machined metal box, often aluminium, that holds microwave photons for a long time. It is used as a long-lived memory or bosonic qubit.
A qubit encoded in the many energy levels of a harmonic oscillator, such as a microwave cavity, allowing built-in error protection.
A lossy auxiliary mode used to engineer interactions, for example to remove photons in pairs from a cat-qubit storage cavity, which stabilizes the cat states.
Keeping a resonator in cat states by continuously driving and removing photons in pairs, which protects the qubit from bit flips.
A system in which an atom or qubit interacts strongly with photons in a cavity. Circuit QED is its superconducting version.
Equipment and control used to create Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill states in oscillators, such as cavities coupled to transmons or trapped-ion motion.
An effect in which a mode's frequency depends on how many photons it holds. It is used to create and protect bosonic states but can also distort them.
A vibrating structure, such as a tiny membrane or beam, whose vibrations (phonons) can be controlled quantum mechanically and used as a memory or bosonic mode.
A continuous drive applied to a bosonic mode to keep its state in a protected subspace, such as the pumping that stabilizes cat qubits.
A long-lived resonator that stores quantum information, often as a bosonic qubit, while a separate transmon controls it.
A superconducting circuit that oscillates at a microwave frequency with very low loss. It is used to read out qubits and store bosonic states.
Engineered loss that removes photons in pairs from a resonator, which drives it toward cat states and suppresses bit flips in cat qubits.
An electronic device that turns an analog signal, such as a readout waveform, into digital numbers for processing.
A custom chip designed for one task, such as fast, low-power qubit control or decoding.
An instrument that outputs voltage waveforms of any shape, used to generate the precisely shaped pulses that control qubits.
A control pulse whose envelope follows a raised cosine shape, smooth at the start and end, which limits spectral leakage to other transitions.
Adjusting control signals to cancel crosstalk, for example by applying small opposite corrections to neighbouring qubits' lines.
An electronic device that turns digital numbers into an analog voltage, used to generate qubit control pulses.
A qubit control pulse with an added derivative component that suppresses leakage to the third level and phase errors.
A reconfigurable chip used to run fast, low-latency control and feedback logic for qubits, such as real-time decoding.
A control pulse with a bell-shaped envelope, commonly used for qubit gates because its smooth edges limit spectral spread.
A short burst of microwave radiation that rotates a qubit, the standard way to perform gates on superconducting and spin qubits.
Tuning the amplitude, frequency, duration and shape of control pulses so gates rotate qubits exactly as intended.
The shape of a control pulse's amplitude over time, such as Gaussian or DRAG, which affects gate speed and errors.
An instrument or circuit that produces the timed control pulses applied to qubits.
The layers of hardware and software that turn a quantum program into pulses and read back results, from compilers down to electronics.
The part of a control system that generates, times and sequences pulses for qubits, and processes their measurements.
Electronics that react to measurement results within the qubits' coherence time, enabling feedback and dynamic circuits.
The part of a control system that plays pulses and instructions in the right order and timing, including branching on measurement results.
A control pulse that switches on and off abruptly. It is simple, but its sharp edges spread energy across many frequencies.
A small bath of pumped liquid helium-4 at about 1.5 kelvin in some dilution refrigerators, used to condense the helium mixture.
The stage of a cryostat at about 4 kelvin, where cryogenic amplifiers and many filters are mounted.
The first cooling stage of a cryostat, at about 50 kelvin, which intercepts heat from room temperature.
A shield made of aluminium, which becomes superconducting at low temperature and blocks magnetic fields from reaching qubits.
The lowest temperature a cryostat reaches, typically about 10 millikelvin for a dilution refrigerator used with superconducting qubits.
A cable with a central conductor inside a cylindrical shield, used to carry microwave signals to and from qubits in the cryostat.
An attenuator mounted on a cold stage of the cryostat, which reduces signal strength and blocks thermal noise from reaching qubits.
A metal rod or plate that conducts heat away from a sample to a cold stage, keeping it cool.
A plate in a dilution refrigerator, at about 100 millikelvin, where components such as attenuators are anchored.
The process of cooling a cryostat from room temperature to its base temperature, which can take a day or more.
How much heat a cryostat stage can remove while holding its temperature, which limits how much wiring and electronics it can support.
A filter on the cryostat wiring that blocks high-frequency noise and infrared radiation from reaching qubits.
The nested layers of radiation and magnetic shields around the qubits inside a cryostat.
A device that cools its contents to very low temperatures. Dilution refrigerators are the kind used for superconducting and spin qubits.
A cryostat that reaches about 10 millikelvin by mixing helium-3 and helium-4. It is essential for superconducting and spin qubits.
The heat entering a cryostat stage, for example through wiring and signals. It must stay below the stage's cooling power.
The mixture of two helium isotopes used in dilution refrigerators. Moving helium-3 across the boundary between the two phases absorbs heat.
The cables and components that carry microwave control and readout signals between room temperature and the qubits.
The coldest part of a dilution refrigerator, where helium-3 crosses between the two phases of the mixture and absorbs heat.
The plate attached to the mixing chamber, the coldest stage, where the quantum chip is mounted.
A shield made of a nickel-iron alloy with very high magnetic permeability, used to block external magnetic fields from qubits.
A superconducting cable that carries signals between cold stages with very little heat conduction.
A structure on a chip that absorbs stray vibrations (phonons), for example after a radiation strike, before they reach qubits and create quasiparticles.
A cryocooler that uses oscillating helium gas pressure to reach about 3 to 4 kelvin, with no moving parts at the cold end. It provides the first cooling stages of modern dry fridges.
A region, often of normal metal or lower-gap superconductor, that captures quasiparticles and keeps them away from qubits' junctions.
The chamber in a dilution refrigerator, at about 0.7 kelvin, where helium-3 evaporates from the mixture and is pumped away.
column3: In everyday English, still means motionless; a still is also an apparatus for distilling.

column2: A point where a cable or component is firmly connected to a cold stage so it cools to that temperature and does not carry heat further down.
Bringing a component or signal to the temperature of its surroundings, so it does not carry excess heat or noise to the qubits.
Measures that stop mechanical vibrations, for example from pumps, reaching the qubits, where they could cause heating or noise.
Bringing a cryostat back from its base temperature to room temperature, for example to change hardware.
Diamond grown by chemical vapour deposition, which can be made very pure for hosting defect-centre qubits.
A piece of diamond hosting colour-centre qubits such as NV or SiV centres.
A defect in diamond made of a germanium atom next to vacancies. It emits bright, stable light, useful for quantum networks.
Nuclear spins near a defect or atom that interact with its electron spin through the hyperfine interaction, so they can be controlled and used as memories.
Diamond grown mostly from carbon-12, removing the carbon-13 nuclear spins that cause noise for defect qubits.
Controlling a defect's electron spin with microwave pulses, the usual way to perform gates on NV-centre qubits.
A group of nuclear spins around a defect, such as carbon-13 near an NV centre, used as long-lived qubits controlled through the defect.
A nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond: a nitrogen atom next to a missing carbon. Its electron spin can be read with light even at room temperature.
Using laser light to initialize, control or read out a defect's spin state.
Reading a defect's spin state from changes in its fluorescence while sweeping microwaves, the standard way to operate NV centres.
A defect in diamond made of a silicon atom between two vacancies. It emits narrow, stable light, useful for quantum networking.
The emission of one photon at a time by a defect such as an NV centre, making defects useful as single-photon sources.
The difference in fluorescence between a defect's spin states, which determines how well they can be distinguished in readout.
A system that links a spin qubit to photons, so its state can be transferred to light for networking.
A defect in diamond made of a tin atom and vacancies. It keeps its coherence at somewhat higher temperatures than the silicon-vacancy centre.
Low-power transistor logic designed to run at cryogenic temperatures by recovering the energy used for switching, proposed for control electronics near qubits.
A digital-to-analog converter built in CMOS and run at cryogenic temperatures near the qubits, reducing wiring from room temperature.
A superconducting circuit that produces precise, quantized voltage pulses to control qubits, developed at NIST.
IBM's planned design of linked modules, each storing logical qubits in bivariate bicycle codes, connected by couplers to form a larger fault-tolerant machine.
Superconducting digital logic that represents bits as tiny, quantized voltage pulses. It is very fast and could control qubits inside the cryostat.
Dedicated electronics, such as FPGAs or ASICs, that decode error-correction syndromes fast enough to keep up with the qubits.
Controlling qubits with trains of single-flux-quantum pulses from superconducting logic placed near the chip, instead of microwaves from room temperature.
Stacking chips or layers vertically and connecting them, so wiring and control can reach qubits from above instead of the chip's edges.
column3: In classical chip design, 3D integration means the same kind of stacking.

column2: A thin metal bridge that arches over another line on a chip, connecting ground planes and suppressing unwanted modes.
The thin insulating layer of aluminium oxide between two aluminium films that forms a Josephson junction.
Heating a fabricated device in a controlled way to change its properties, for example to adjust Josephson junction resistance.
column3: In quantum computing, quantum annealing is an unrelated method of optimization.

column2: A method of depositing extremely thin, uniform films one atomic layer at a time, used for insulators and barriers.
Joining two chips face to face with small metal bumps, used in flip-chip designs to connect qubits to wiring layers.
A room with tightly controlled dust, temperature and humidity, needed to fabricate qubit chips without defects.
A structure that lets one line on a chip cross over another without connecting, such as an air bridge.
column3: In other fields, crossover has many meanings, such as a point where two trends meet.

column2: A suspended strip of resist that lets a Josephson junction be made by evaporating metal from two angles in one step.
Depositing metal from two angles, with an oxidation step between, to form a Josephson junction through a resist mask.
Patterning very fine features by writing with a focused electron beam in a resist, used to define Josephson junctions and quantum dots.
Mounting one chip face down on another and connecting them with bumps, separating qubits from their wiring layer.
A large area of metal on a chip held at ground potential, which shields circuits and provides a return path for signals.
A patterning method in which metal is deposited over a patterned resist and then the resist is dissolved, leaving metal only where the resist was open.
A Josephson junction made by evaporating metal along two perpendicular directions, avoiding the suspended bridge of the Dolan method.
A chip built from several layers of metal and insulator, allowing wiring to cross and route signals to many qubits.
A layer of niobium, a superconductor, used for a chip's wiring, resonators and ground plane.
A superconducting compound used for single-photon detectors and high-kinetic-inductance resonators.
A superconducting compound with high kinetic inductance, used in resonators, single-photon detectors and some qubit designs.
Patterning features on a chip by shining light through a mask onto a light-sensitive resist, the standard method for larger features.
A method of etching materials with reactive gas ions in a plasma, used to carve precise features into films and substrates.
A crystalline aluminium oxide base for qubit chips, valued for its low microwave loss.
A silicon wafer used as the base for qubit chips, compatible with standard semiconductor manufacturing.
A method of depositing thin films by knocking atoms off a target with ions, used to lay down superconducting metals such as niobium.
A layer of tantalum used for superconducting qubits, whose cleaner surface oxide gives lower loss and longer coherence.
A vertical metal connection passing through a silicon chip, used to route signals in 3D-integrated quantum processors.
Making many chips at once on full wafers with industrial processes, improving uniformity and scale.
The quantum device or simulator that actually runs a circuit, such as a particular processor offered through a cloud service.
column3: In software, the backend is the server side of an application.

column2: A graph showing which qubits can interact directly on a device.
The instruments and circuits that generate the signals controlling qubits and process their readout.
A list or graph of which qubit pairs can perform two-qubit gates directly on a device, used by compilers.
A wire or waveguide that carries control pulses to a qubit.
A transmission line shared by several readout resonators, through which they are all measured.
A line carrying current near a superconducting qubit's loop to tune its frequency or activate gates with magnetic flux.
The two-qubit gate a device performs directly, such as CZ, iSWAP or cross-resonance. Other two-qubit gates are built from it.
A chip carrying qubits and their couplers, resonators and wiring, the physical heart of a quantum processor.
The part of a quantum computer that holds and operates the qubits, analogous to a CPU.
A group of qubits treated together to hold a quantum value, such as an n-qubit number.
The hardware and software that pass information between qubits and classical electronics, such as control signals and measurement results.
The physical technology used to build qubits, such as superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons or spins.
The electronics that generate readout signals, amplify and digitize the responses, and turn them into qubit measurement results.
The transmission line carrying readout signals from the qubits' resonators out of the cryostat.
An instrument that measures the shape and size of a laser beam, used to align optical systems for atoms and ions.
A thermometer that measures very low temperatures inside a cryostat, using sensors such as ruthenium oxide or Cernox.
An instrument that generates stable signals at precisely set frequencies, used for qubit control and readout.
A vacuum pump that removes gas by ionizing it and burying the ions in metal. It is used to keep trapped-ion and atom systems in ultra-high vacuum.
An instrument that extracts a small signal at a known frequency from noise, used for sensitive measurements.
A device, such as a fluxgate or Hall probe, that measures magnetic fields around an experiment.
An instrument that displays voltage signals over time, used to inspect control pulses and readout signals.
A semiconductor device that turns light into current, used to monitor laser power and detect photons.
An instrument that produces electrical signals, such as microwave tones, for qubit control or testing.
An instrument that shows how a signal's power is spread across frequencies, used to check for noise and spurious tones.
A high-speed vacuum pump with spinning blades that knock gas molecules out, used to reach high vacuum.
An instrument that measures pressure inside a vacuum system.
An instrument that measures how a device transmits and reflects signals across frequencies, used to characterize resonators and qubits.
A heavy table with vibration dampers that keeps lasers and optics stable, essential for atom and ion experiments.
Moving trapped atoms with optical tweezers to fill gaps and form defect-free arrays.
The distance within which one Rydberg atom prevents another from being excited to a Rydberg state. It sets which atoms can be entangled.
An alkali atom used in neutral-atom quantum computers and atomic clocks. The second is defined by a caesium transition.
A pair of atomic states whose energy difference is insensitive to magnetic fields, or the long-lived states used in optical clocks, giving qubits with long coherence.
A laser beam used to slow and cool atoms or ions.
Two acousto-optic deflectors at right angles, which steer a laser beam in two dimensions to make or move a grid of optical tweezers.
Arranging atoms into an array with no empty sites, usually by rearranging them with tweezers after random loading.
A set of optical tweezers that can move during an experiment, used to rearrange atoms and bring them together for gates.
Detecting when a qubit has left its computational states, turning an unknown error into an erasure, which is easier to correct.
A glass vacuum chamber that gives clear optical access to trapped atoms or ions.
A laser used to make atoms fluoresce so a camera can see them, used to detect atom positions and read out states.
Slowing atoms or ions by making them absorb and re-emit laser light many times, cooling them to microkelvin temperatures.
A trap that uses laser beams and a magnetic field gradient to cool and collect a cloud of cold atoms, the first step in atom experiments.
A long-lived excited state that decays slowly. Some neutral-atom and ion qubits are stored in metastable states.
column3: In physics generally, a metastable state is one that is stable for a long time but not the lowest-energy state.

column2: A qubit stored in the internal states of an uncharged atom held in an optical tweezer.
A periodic pattern of light, made by interfering laser beams, that traps atoms at regular sites like eggs in a carton.
A tightly focused laser beam that traps a single atom at its focus, used to build and rearrange atom arrays.
The number n labelling an electron's main energy level. Rydberg states have large n, often above 50, which makes atoms huge.
Loading atoms into a reservoir region and then moving them into the working array as needed, to refill lost atoms.
An alkali atom widely used in neutral-atom quantum computers and cold-atom experiments.
The effect in which one atom excited to a Rydberg state shifts its neighbours' Rydberg levels so they cannot be excited. It is used to make two-qubit gates.
Mixing a small amount of a Rydberg state into an atom's ground state with off-resonant light, giving weaker but longer-lived interactions.
A highly excited atomic state with a large principal quantum number, in which the atom is huge and interacts strongly with its neighbours.
A two-qubit gate between neutral atoms that uses the strong interaction of Rydberg states, such as the blockade.
A device that shapes laser light pixel by pixel, used to create many optical tweezers at once.
A fixed pattern of optical tweezers holding atoms in place.
The probability that an atom or qubit is still present, or in the intended state, after an operation.
A laser beam that holds atoms in place, as in an optical tweezer or lattice.
A set of many optical tweezers, each holding one atom, forming the register of a neutral-atom quantum computer.
Changing the positions of tweezers during an experiment to move atoms, for example to fill gaps or connect distant qubits.
Exciting an atom with two laser photons whose energies add up, used to reach Rydberg states through an intermediate level.
A chamber pumped to extremely low pressure, so collisions with leftover gas rarely disturb trapped atoms or ions.
The sealed, evacuated chamber, often glass, in which atoms or ions are trapped and controlled.
A photodiode with internal gain from an avalanche of electrons, which can detect weak light or single photons.
An optical element that splits a beam into two, transmitting part and reflecting part. It is the basic interferometric element in photonic quantum computing.
Light lost when coupling between components, such as from a fibre into a chip. It is a major limit for photonic systems.
How often a photon detector clicks when no photon is present, which adds false signals.
The probability that a detector registers a photon that reaches it.
A structure that couples light into or out of a photonic chip through its edge, often with low loss over a wide range of wavelengths.
A component that changes the phase of light by applying a voltage to an electro-optic material, which can switch very fast.
An optical cavity made of two facing mirrors between which light bounces back and forth, enhancing its interaction with atoms or emitters.
Transferring light between an optical fibre and a photonic chip, where loss must be minimized.
A photon pair source that uses a nonlinear process in which two pump photons convert into a signal and an idler photon, common in silicon photonics.
A patterned structure on a photonic chip that diffracts light between the chip and a fibre above it.
A source that produces photon pairs and detects one photon to announce (herald) that its partner exists.
Photonic integrated circuits built on indium phosphide, which can include lasers and amplifiers on the same chip.
An interferometer that splits light into two paths and recombines it. With phase shifters, it acts as a tunable beam splitter in photonic circuits.
A tiny ring-shaped waveguide in which light circulates many times, used as a filter, modulator or photon-pair source.
A waveguide wide enough to carry several spatial modes of light.
An arrangement of mirrors or structures that traps light, enhancing its interaction with atoms or emitters.
A path, often a long fibre or waveguide, that delays light by a set time, used to synchronize photons.
A device that routes light between paths, needed for feed-forward in photonic quantum computing.
A source in which a nonlinear crystal splits one pump photon into two lower-energy photons, producing entangled or heralded photon pairs.
Lithium niobate with a periodically flipped crystal structure, which makes nonlinear processes such as down-conversion efficient.
A component that changes the phase of light in a waveguide, used to program photonic circuits.
A detector's ability to count how many photons arrive, not just whether any did. It is needed for some photonic protocols.
A cavity formed by a periodic pattern of holes in a material, which traps light in a tiny volume.
A chip that routes and processes light in waveguides, beam splitters and phase shifters, the photonic counterpart of an electronic chip.
The fraction of photons lost in a photonic system, through absorption, scattering or poor coupling. It is the main source of errors in photonic computing.
A qubit encoded in a photon, for example in its polarization, path or arrival time.
A beam splitter that transmits one polarization and reflects the other, used to measure polarization-encoded qubits.
An optical fibre that preserves the polarization of light along its length.
A semiconductor quantum dot that emits one photon at a time when excited, producing bright, identical single photons.
Photonic circuits made from silicon nitride, which has very low loss and is used for sources, filters and delay lines.
Photonic circuits made in silicon with standard chip manufacturing, used by several photonic quantum computing efforts.
A waveguide that carries only one spatial mode of light, which is needed for clean interference between photons.
A photodiode biased so that a single photon triggers an avalanche, allowing it to detect individual photons.
How often a single-photon source delivers a photon into the collection path per excitation, which sets achievable rates.
A superconducting nanowire single-photon detector: a thin superconducting wire that briefly loses superconductivity when hit by a photon. It is highly efficient and fast.
A source that produces light with reduced noise in one quadrature, used for continuous-variable photonic computing and sensing.
Photonic circuits made from tantalum pentoxide, a material with low loss and useful nonlinear properties.
A component that changes light's phase by heating a waveguide, changing its refractive index. It is common but slower than electro-optic shifters.
A thin layer of lithium niobate on an insulator, used to make fast, low-loss electro-optic modulators and nonlinear photonic circuits.
Random variation in when a detector or source registers an event, which limits how precisely photons can be timed and synchronized.
column3: In electronics generally, jitter is timing variation in any signal.

column2: A superconducting detector kept at the edge of its superconducting transition, where absorbing a photon changes its resistance measurably. It can count photons.
A structure that confines and guides light or microwaves along a path, such as an optical fibre, a photonic chip channel or a metal tube.
A superconducting nanowire single-photon detector built directly on top of a photonic waveguide, absorbing photons as they travel along it.
A waveguide junction shaped like a Y that splits light from one path into two.
Returning a qubit to |0⟩ quickly by measuring it and applying a flip if needed, instead of waiting for it to relax.
A thin wire, often aluminium, that connects pads on a chip to its package or circuit board.
A device that routes microwave signals in one direction around a loop of ports, used to separate outgoing readout signals from incoming ones and block noise.
A device that splits off part of a signal travelling in one direction, used to combine or sample signals in control and readout lines.
Measuring a qubit through the small, state-dependent frequency shift it causes in a coupled resonator, without directly exciting the qubit. It is standard for superconducting qubits.
Shifting a high-frequency signal to a lower frequency by mixing it with a local oscillator, so it can be digitized and processed.
column3: In optics, down-conversion instead means splitting one photon into two.

column2: A filter containing Eccosorb, a lossy absorbing material, that removes infrared and high-frequency radiation from cryogenic signal lines.
A high-electron-mobility transistor amplifier at about 4 kelvin, which boosts faint readout signals with low added noise.
Measuring a signal by mixing it with a slightly different frequency, which captures both of its quadratures at once.
Measuring a signal by mixing it with a reference at the same frequency, which captures one chosen quadrature.
A filter that blocks infrared radiation from reaching qubits, where it would break Cooper pairs and create quasiparticles.
A mixer that combines a signal with in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components of a local oscillator, used to shape pulses and demodulate readout.
A device that lets microwave signals pass in one direction only, protecting qubits from noise travelling back down the readout line.
A superconducting amplifier based on Josephson junctions that boosts faint readout signals while adding almost the minimum noise quantum mechanics allows.
A parametric amplifier that uses the nonlinear kinetic inductance of thin superconducting films, which can handle larger signals than junction-based amplifiers.
A spin readout method in which the spin state is converted into a charge state that stays locked in place, allowing a longer, more reliable measurement.
A stable reference signal mixed with other signals to shift their frequency, used in generating and reading qubit signals.
Enclosures made of materials such as mu-metal or superconductors that block external magnetic fields from reaching qubits.
Reading out several qubits at once through one shared line, each through its own resonator at a different frequency.
A connector that presses spring-loaded pins onto a chip's pads, giving many signal connections without wire bonds.
A readout that leaves the qubit in the state it reported, so measuring again gives the same answer.
An amplifier that adds only the minimum noise quantum mechanics allows, such as a Josephson parametric amplifier, needed for fast, accurate readout.
The package that holds a quantum chip in the cryostat, providing electrical connections, shielding and cooling.
The part that holds and thermally anchors a quantum chip or its package inside the cryostat.
Determining a qubit's state from one measurement, without averaging over repetitions. It is needed for error correction.
A broadband quantum-limited amplifier made of a long chain of Josephson junctions, which can amplify many readout channels at once.
Shifting a low-frequency signal to a higher frequency by mixing it with a local oscillator, used to create qubit control pulses.
column3: In optics, up-conversion means combining photons into higher-energy ones.

column2: Connecting a chip's pads to its package or board with thin bonded wires.
A region of electrons, such as a doped lead, from which a quantum dot is filled or emptied.
A sensitive device, such as a single-electron transistor, placed next to quantum dots to detect changes in their electron number.
A change in the number of electrons on a quantum dot, seen as a line in a stability diagram.
Making qubit devices, especially silicon spin qubits, in industrial semiconductor factories using standard chip processes.
Ordinary CMOS electronics designed to operate at cryogenic temperatures near the qubits, reducing wiring and latency.
A qubit stored in the spin of an electron or nucleus of a single donor atom, such as phosphorus, placed in silicon.
Controlling an electron spin with oscillating electric fields, which works through spin-orbit coupling or a nearby micromagnet.
Controlling or measuring electron spins by driving transitions between spin states with microwaves in a magnetic field.
A single-shot spin readout in which a spin-up electron can tunnel out of the dot and a spin-down one cannot, detected by a charge sensor.
The quantum interaction between neighbouring electron spins caused by the overlap of their wavefunctions. It is used to make two-qubit gates between spin qubits.
A spin qubit encoded in three electrons, fully controlled with voltage-driven exchange interactions, so no microwave or magnetic fields are needed.
A spin qubit in which an electron is spread over two quantum dots, making it couple strongly to electric fields and microwave photons.
A quantum dot created by voltages on metal gates above a semiconductor, which confine single electrons or holes.
A spin qubit using the spin of a hole, a missing electron, often in germanium. Strong spin-orbit coupling allows fast electrical control.
Spin qubits operated at around 1 kelvin or above, rather than millikelvin, where cryogenic electronics have much more cooling power.
A spin qubit using three electrons in a double quantum dot, combining spin and charge properties for fast electrical control.
column3: The term is also used for any qubit combining two physical systems.

column2: Silicon enriched in silicon-28, which has no nuclear spin, removing a major source of noise for spin qubits.
The original spin qubit proposal (1998): a single electron spin in a quantum dot, with exchange interactions between neighbours for two-qubit gates.
A tiny magnet placed near quantum dots to create a magnetic field gradient, letting electric fields drive and address individual spin qubits.
A metal-oxide-semiconductor layered structure, as in ordinary transistors, used to form quantum dots in silicon.
The blocking of current or charge movement between two quantum dots when electrons have parallel spins, used to read out spin qubits.
A tiny region of a semiconductor that confines electrons so they have discrete energy levels, like an artificial atom. It can hold spin qubits or emit single photons.
A narrow constriction in a two-dimensional electron gas whose conductance is very sensitive to nearby charges, used as a charge sensor.
A single-electron transistor read out with radio-frequency signals, allowing fast and sensitive charge sensing.
Layers of silicon and silicon-germanium that trap electrons in a thin silicon layer, a common host for spin qubits.
A qubit stored in the spin of an electron or hole in silicon, compatible with chip manufacturing and potentially very dense.
A small island that exchanges single electrons with a reservoir through one tunnel junction, used as a compact charge sensor in gate-based readout.
A transistor whose current depends on single electrons tunnelling on and off a tiny island, making it an extremely sensitive charge sensor.
A spin qubit encoded in two electrons, using their singlet and triplet spin states, which can be controlled with voltages.
Turning a spin state into a charge configuration that can be detected, the basis of most spin qubit readout.
A map of a quantum dot device's charge states as two gate voltages are swept, used to tune dots to hold single electrons.
A bias condition for exchange-coupled spin qubits where the exchange is first-order insensitive to charge noise, reducing errors.
Electrons confined to a thin layer at a semiconductor interface, free to move in two dimensions. Quantum dots and point contacts are made in it.
A Josephson junction made of two aluminium films separated by a thin aluminium oxide barrier, the standard junction in superconducting qubits.
A superconducting qubit based on Andreev bound states, electron states localized in a weak link between two superconductors, such as a nanowire junction.
An oscillator whose energy levels are unevenly spaced. The uneven spacing lets its two lowest levels be addressed as a qubit, as in the transmon.
A SQUID with two Josephson junctions of different sizes. Used in tunable transmons, it limits the tuning range and lowers sensitivity to flux noise.
A tunable transmon whose SQUID has unequal junctions, giving two flux sweet spots and reduced sensitivity to flux noise.
A filter that lets through only signals near the readout frequency, protecting a qubit from decaying into the readout line.
A superconducting qubit that combines a fluxonium-like loop with a Cooper-pair box, protecting it against certain errors through parity.
A resonator shared by several qubits that mediates interactions between them.
A flux qubit with a large added capacitor, which reduces its sensitivity to charge noise and improves coherence.
A flux qubit with a shunt capacitor that reduces charge noise sensitivity and improves reproducibility, the same as a C-shunt flux qubit.
A qubit stored in cat states of a resonator, superpositions of two coherent states. Bit flips are suppressed exponentially, leaving mainly phase flips to correct.
A superconducting qubit whose states differ by the number of Cooper pairs on an island. Early versions suffered from charge noise; the transmon fixed this.
The energy cost of adding one electron (or Cooper pair) to a superconducting island, EC. Its ratio to the Josephson energy sets a qubit's properties.
A pair of electrons bound together in a superconductor. Cooper pairs carry current without resistance and make superconducting qubits possible.
A small superconducting island connected by a Josephson junction, whose states differ by the number of Cooper pairs. It was an early charge qubit.
A protected superconducting qubit whose states differ in the parity of the number of Cooper pairs, making it insensitive to many kinds of noise.
A transmission line with a central conductor between two ground planes on the same surface, used to make resonators and lines on qubit chips.
A resonator made from a length of coplanar waveguide, used for qubit readout and coupling.
A circuit element that connects qubits so they can interact, which may be fixed or tunable.
A qubit encoded in which of two resonators or transmons holds a single excitation, so that energy loss becomes a detectable erasure.
A permanent coupling, such as a capacitor, between two qubits. It is simple but causes always-on interactions.
A transmon with a single Josephson junction, so its frequency cannot be tuned. It avoids flux noise but needs microwave-only gates.
A constant or slowly varying magnetic flux applied to a superconducting loop to set a qubit's or coupler's frequency.
A fast change in the magnetic flux through a qubit's or coupler's loop, used to tune its frequency briefly, for example to perform a CZ gate.
The smallest unit of magnetic flux in a superconducting loop, h/2e, about 2.07 × 10⁻¹⁵ webers.
A superconducting qubit whose states correspond to current circulating clockwise or anticlockwise in a loop with Josephson junctions.
A flux bias at which a qubit's frequency is insensitive to first order to flux changes, reducing dephasing from flux noise.
A superconducting qubit made of a Josephson junction shunted by a very large inductance. It has low frequency, large anharmonicity and very long coherence.
A Google superconducting qubit design with a tunable inductive coupler, allowing qubit interactions to be switched on and off.
A superconductor made of tiny aluminium grains in oxide, with high kinetic inductance, used for superinductors in qubits such as fluxonium.
A fluxonium with a large capacitance, giving a very low frequency and long lifetime, controlled with special techniques.
The energy scale EJ of a Josephson junction, set by how easily Cooper pairs tunnel across it. With charging energy, it sets a qubit's behaviour.
Two superconductors separated by a thin barrier, through which Cooper pairs tunnel. It provides the nonlinearity that makes superconducting qubits possible.
Inductance caused by the inertia of moving Cooper pairs, large in thin or disordered superconductors, used to make compact resonators and superinductors.
A multi-mode coupler from IBM whose engineered multi-path interference cancels unwanted qubit coupling over a wide frequency range, without flux tuning.
A resonator made from separate compact capacitor and inductor elements, instead of a length of transmission line.
A metal box or resonant structure that confines microwave photons, used for qubit readout, coupling or as a long-lived memory.
A Josephson junction made with niobium electrodes, common in superconducting electronics but less used in qubits than aluminium junctions.
A filter that blocks signals at the qubit's frequency on the readout line, preventing the qubit from decaying through it.
A coupler whose parameters are modulated at a chosen frequency to turn on specific interactions between qubits on demand.
An early superconducting qubit based on a current-biased Josephson junction, whose states are levels in a tilted potential well.
A filter between a qubit's readout resonator and the output line that allows fast readout while preventing the qubit from decaying through it.
A potential energy that grows with the fourth power of a variable. Some superconducting circuits use it to give qubits particular energy level spacings.
A variable in some superconducting circuits, dual to the phase across a junction, that plays the role of charge in describing Bloch-band states.
A resonator coupled to a qubit whose frequency shifts depending on the qubit's state, used to measure it.
A capacitor placed in parallel with a Josephson junction, which lowers the charging energy and makes the qubit insensitive to charge noise, as in the transmon.
The minimum energy needed to break a Cooper pair in a superconductor. It protects qubits from excitations, and breaking pairs creates quasiparticles.
A superconducting loop with one or two Josephson junctions, extremely sensitive to magnetic flux. It is used as a magnetometer and to tune qubits.
A qubit built from superconducting circuits with Josephson junctions, cooled to millikelvin temperatures. Transmons are the most common kind.
A tunable transmon whose SQUID has two equal junctions, giving a wide tuning range but greater sensitivity to flux noise away from the sweet spot.
The most widely used superconducting qubit: a Josephson junction shunted by a large capacitor, which makes it insensitive to charge noise.
A coupler whose strength can be adjusted, typically with flux, so qubits interact during gates and are isolated otherwise.
A transmon with a SQUID in place of a single junction, so its frequency can be tuned with magnetic flux.
A transmon design from Google shaped like a cross, allowing connections to control lines, readout and other qubits on its arms.
A protected superconducting qubit whose two states are separated in the circuit's phase, designed to be intrinsically resistant to both relaxation and dephasing.
Aluminium grown on a semiconductor, such as an InAs nanowire, which induces superconductivity in it through the proximity effect. It is used for Majorana devices.
Exchanging anyons, such as Majorana zero modes, around each other to perform a gate that depends only on the topology of the exchange.
A combination of indium arsenide semiconductor and aluminium superconductor, the main material platform for Majorana-based topological qubits.
A thin semiconductor wire of indium arsenide which, coated with a superconductor and placed in a magnetic field, can host Majorana zero modes.
A measurement that detects a phase difference between paths. In Majorana devices, it is used to read out the fermion parity of the qubit.
A qubit encoded non-locally in several Majorana zero modes, so local noise cannot easily disturb it. It is the basis of topological quantum computing.
A quasiparticle state at the end of a topological superconductor that is its own antiparticle. Pairs of them store qubit information non-locally.
column3: Majorana fermions in particle physics are the related elementary particles proposed by Ettore Majorana.

column2: Measuring whether a system has an even or odd number of fermions, which is how Majorana qubits are read out.
Reading out a Majorana qubit's parity through a quantum dot coupled to it, whose response depends on that parity.
A nanowire of semiconductor coated with a superconductor, engineered to become a topological superconductor hosting Majorana modes.
Microsoft's topological qubit design: two parallel topological nanowires joined by a superconducting link, together hosting four Majorana zero modes.
Microsoft's name for its topological superconductor material, used in its Majorana 1 chip announced in 2025.
The energy gap that protects a topological phase. Its size sets how well Majorana modes are shielded from noise.
A test procedure proposed by Microsoft to decide whether a device has entered a topological phase with Majorana modes. Its reliability has been debated.
A qubit whose information is stored in the global, topological properties of a system, making it inherently resistant to local noise.
A superconductor with a topological phase that hosts Majorana zero modes at its ends or edges.
A device that steers a laser beam by bouncing it off sound waves in a crystal, used to move optical tweezers or address individual ions.
A device that uses sound waves in a crystal to switch, shift the frequency of, or shape a laser beam quickly, used to pulse lasers in ion and atom experiments.
The oscillation frequency of trapped ions along the trap's long axis.
An ion species used as a trapped-ion qubit. Its visible transitions work well with standard optics and fibres.
Optical elements that direct laser beams precisely onto individual ions or atoms.
A light ion species used in trapped-ion experiments, often for logic gates or as a cooling partner for other ions.
A laser beam containing two frequencies, used in the Mølmer–Sørensen gate to drive red and blue motional sidebands together.
A linear Paul trap made of four blade-shaped electrodes pointing at the ions, giving good optical access.
A collective motion of trapped ions in which they move symmetrically toward and away from the centre.
A common trapped-ion species, used for optical and hyperfine qubits and addressed with lasers at convenient wavelengths.
A transition that changes an ion's internal state without changing its motional state, used for single-qubit gates.
The motion in which all ions in a chain move together in the same direction. It is often used to mediate two-qubit gates.
A collective motion shared by all ions in a trap, such as the centre-of-mass mode, which couples their qubits for gates.
An electrode used to cancel stray electric fields so ions sit at the trap's field-free point, minimizing micromotion.
A trap electrode with a static voltage that confines ions along the trap axis and moves them between zones.
A laser that makes ions in one qubit state fluoresce and not the other, so the state can be read out with a detector.
A laser tuned slightly below an atomic transition that slows moving ions or atoms through the Doppler effect.
A chain of trapped ions of two different elements, one for computation and the other for cooling or networking without disturbing the qubits.
Electromagnetically induced transparency cooling: a laser cooling method that cools several motional modes of trapped ions quickly to near the ground state.
A device that changes the phase or amplitude of light with an electric field, used to add sidebands or modulate lasers.
An electron-multiplying CCD camera, sensitive enough to detect a few photons, used to image fluorescence from ions or atoms.
Reading out a qubit by shining a laser that makes one state glow and the other stay dark, then detecting the emitted light.
A laser whose spectrum is a comb of evenly spaced frequencies, used to drive Raman gates in ions and to compare atomic clocks.
A laser beam that illuminates all ions or atoms at once, used for operations applied to every qubit.
A qubit stored in two hyperfine levels of an atom or ion's ground state, which have very long coherence times.
Optics that focus laser beams tightly onto single ions or atoms, so each qubit can be controlled separately.
A line of ions held in a trap, repelling each other, whose shared motion connects their qubits.
A string of trapped ions arranged in a straight line along the trap axis.
A Paul trap with electrodes along a line, confining ions radially with radio-frequency fields and axially with static fields, so they form a chain.
A light ion species used in trapped-ion experiments, often as a cooling or logic partner ion.
An ion trap made with chip fabrication techniques, allowing complex electrode layouts and many trapping zones.
A small, fast jiggling of a trapped ion driven by the trap's radio-frequency field, which can cause errors if not minimized.
A transition that changes both an ion's internal state and its motional state, used for cooling and for two-qubit gates.
The two-frequency laser or microwave drive that implements the Mølmer–Sørensen entangling gate between trapped ions.
Delivering laser light to a trap through optical fibres, which improves stability and scalability.
A qubit stored in two levels of an ion or atom separated by an optical frequency, controlled with narrow-linewidth lasers.
A trap that holds charged particles using oscillating radio-frequency electric fields. It is the standard ion trap and earned Wolfgang Paul a Nobel Prize.
A trap that confines charged particles using a strong magnetic field combined with static electric fields. It can hold large crystals of ions.
A laser that removes an electron from neutral atoms to create ions for loading into a trap.
A light detector that multiplies electrons produced by incoming photons, sensitive enough to detect single photons from ions.
A Paul trap designed to hold ions at a single point, rather than along a line.
The effective static potential that describes the average force of an oscillating trap field on an ion.
The oscillation frequency of trapped ions in the directions across the trap axis.
A laser cooling technique that uses Raman transitions to remove motional quanta one at a time, cooling atoms or ions to their motional ground state.
A laser that returns atoms or ions from unwanted states back into the cooling or qubit cycle.
Cooling a trapped ion to its motional ground state by driving the transition that also removes one motional quantum.
The trap electrode carrying the radio-frequency voltage that provides radial confinement in a Paul trap.
The line or point in a Paul trap where the radio-frequency field is zero, where ions sit with minimal micromotion.
An ion trap in which ions are held in a ring-shaped configuration.
The frequency of an ion's slow oscillation in a Paul trap's effective potential, as opposed to its fast micromotion.
A trap with many separate electrodes along its axis, so ions can be held in different zones and moved between them.
A transition that changes both an ion's internal state and its motion by one quantum, used for cooling and gates.
A laser that puts atoms or ions into a known starting state, usually by optical pumping.
A collective motion of ions in which they move in opposite directions, stretching and compressing the chain.
An ion species used for trapped-ion qubits and optical clocks.
A trapped-ion chip with all electrodes on one surface, holding ions just above it. It is easier to scale than 3D traps.
An ion trap with all its electrodes on a flat surface, trapping ions tens of micrometres above it, made with chip fabrication.
An ion of a different species in the same trap, cooled by lasers to cool the computing ions through their shared motion without disturbing their qubits.
The energy needed for an ion or atom to escape its trap. Deeper traps hold particles more reliably.
A qubit stored in the internal states of a single trapped ion, controlled with lasers or microwaves. It offers long coherence and high-fidelity gates.
An instrument that measures a laser's wavelength precisely, used to keep lasers tuned to atomic transitions.
A popular trapped-ion species whose hyperfine qubit is very stable and easy to control. It is used by several companies.
A qubit stored in two Zeeman levels of an atom or ion, which split in a magnetic field. It is simple to control but sensitive to field noise.
The change of a trapped-ion chain from a straight line to a zigzag shape when the axial confinement grows relative to the radial.
A series of attenuators at different cryostat stages that reduce signal power and thermal noise on the way down to the qubits.
A filter that passes signals within a frequency band and blocks those outside it.
A metal pad on a chip where wires or bumps are attached to make electrical connections.
The coaxial cables that carry microwave signals through the cryostat to and from the quantum chip.
A thermal connection, often a metal rod, that links a component to a cold stage so it stays cold.
An attenuator designed to work at cryogenic temperatures, reducing signal power and blocking thermal noise.
A printed circuit board designed to work at cryogenic temperatures, routing signals near the quantum chip.
A lossy, magnetically loaded material that absorbs stray microwave and infrared radiation inside cryogenic packaging.
A series of filters on a signal line that together block noise across a wide range of frequencies.
A sealed connector that passes signals through a wall without letting gas through.
A filter that passes low-frequency signals and blocks high-frequency noise.
A printed circuit board with several layers of wiring, needed to route many signals to large quantum chips.
A simple filter made of a resistor and capacitor, used to remove high-frequency noise from DC and flux lines.
A metal enclosure that blocks radio-frequency and microwave interference from reaching sensitive circuits.
The shielded enclosure that holds a quantum chip and its connections inside the cryostat.
A sealed connector that passes electrical or optical signals into a vacuum system.
